---
title: "Generalized linear models"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

A **generalized linear model (GLM)** answers three questions in order:

1. Which values can the response take, and how does its variability behave?
2. Which predictors will we combine, and with which coefficients?
3. How will we translate that predictor combination into the response mean?

These questions give us the model's three parts: a response distribution, a linear predictor, and a link. We have already seen why [binary responses](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd) need a different distribution and how [link functions](link-functions.qmd) translate between scales. We will now fit those pieces together without letting their names obscure their jobs.

The following observed result verb row gives us something concrete to carry through the model:

```{r}
#| label: observed-glm-row
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
st[which(st$verb_type == "result")[[1L]], c(
  "participant_id", "sentence_id", "verb", "verb_type", "preposition", "prep_in"
)]
```

First, $Y_i\in\{0,1\}$ records this participant's *for* or *in* choice. Second, the result indicator equals one, so the predictor sum is $\beta_0+\beta_1$. Third, the inverse logit converts that unrestricted sum into a probability between zero and one. For an observed manner verb row, the indicator equals zero and the same calculation reduces to $\beta_0$. Repeating these operations gives one conditional mean for every row. To obtain the [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd), we evaluate the Bernoulli mass at each observed choice and multiply those masses under the conditional independence assumption.

Recall that a [random variable](../random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd) assigns a numerical value to each possible outcome. A [conditional probability](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd) restricts the comparison to rows with supplied predictor values. When we later multiply row probabilities, we will be using an [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) assumption. And when we report uncertainty, keep the response [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd), which describes variation in choices, separate from a coefficient [standard error](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd), which describes variation in an estimator across hypothetical samples. <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->

| GLM component | General notation | SuperTelicity mapping |
|---|---|---|
| Random component | $Y_i\mid\mu_i$ and its distribution | `prep_in` is $Y_i\in\{0,1\}$; $Y_i\mid\pi_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)$ |
| Conditional mean | $\mu_i=\mathbb{E}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]$ | $\pi_i=\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1\mid\text{verb type}_i)$ |
| Linear predictor | $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta$ | $\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i$ |
| Link | $g(\mu_i)=\eta_i$ | $\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)=\eta_i$ |
| Prediction | $g^{-1}(\eta_i)$ | `plogis(eta)` |
| Variance | $\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mathbf x_i]$ | $\pi_i(1-\pi_i)$ |

The random response $Y_i$ has the Bernoulli distribution. Its parameter $\pi_i$ is an unknown conditional mean determined by the coefficients and predictors; frequentist probability is assigned to the response rather than to this fixed parameter.

```{r}
#| label: fit-supertelicity-glm
#| echo: true
fit <- glm(prep_in ~ verb_type, family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = st)
raw <- aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st, mean)
raw$n <- as.integer(table(st$verb_type))
raw$fitted <- predict(fit, newdata = raw, type = "response")
raw
```

The later [IRLS derivation](iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd) shows how `glm()` searches for the coefficients that maximize this likelihood. For current purposes, we use the resulting coefficients to work out the fitted probabilities.

The response component is $Y_i\mid\pi_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)$, the systematic component is

$$
\eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i,
$$

and the link gives

$$
\log\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}=\eta_i,
\qquad
\pi_i=\frac{1}{1+\exp[-(\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i)]}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: plot-glm-components
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
plot_data <- rbind(
  transform(raw, estimate = prep_in, kind = "observed"),
  transform(raw, estimate = fitted, kind = "fitted")
)
ggplot(plot_data, aes(verb_type, estimate, shape = kind, group = kind)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .18), size = 2.2) +
  labs(x = "Verb type", y = "Probability of an in-completion", shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

The fitted values coincide with the two raw group proportions because a two-parameter model is saturated for two group means. This agreement does not erase the row structure: the likelihood is built from `r nrow(st)` binary choices contributed by repeated participants and sentences.

To see what changes in a nonsaturated model, restrict attention to the episodic rows and add the temporal magnitude selected by the participant. On these rows, the participant supplied a numeral and time unit along with the preposition. Duration and preposition are thus jointly elicited responses. A common duration slope describes how the two recorded choices vary together; it cannot tell us how changing an event's duration would cause the preposition choice to change. The model now estimates fewer cell-specific features than the data could support, so fitted probabilities need not equal every empirical subgroup proportion.

```{r}
#| label: nonsaturated-supertelicity-glm
#| echo: true
st$duration_centered <- st$log_duration_minutes -
  mean(st$log_duration_minutes, na.rm = TRUE)
nonsaturated_rows <- complete.cases(
  st[, c("prep_in", "verb_type", "duration_centered")]
)
stopifnot(
  sum(nonsaturated_rows) == 5380L,
  all(st$clause_type[nonsaturated_rows] == "episodic"),
  all(is.na(st$log_duration_minutes[st$clause_type == "generic"]))
)
nonsaturated <- glm(prep_in ~ verb_type + duration_centered,
                    family = binomial(link = "logit"),
                    data = st[nonsaturated_rows, ])
head(data.frame(observed = st$prep_in[nonsaturated_rows],
                linear_predictor = predict(nonsaturated, type = "link"),
                fitted_probability = predict(nonsaturated, type = "response")))
```

We use this population GLM to work through the response distribution, linear predictor, and link. The SuperTelicity analysis additionally represents dependence among participants and items, so its uncertainty and inferential target differ from the quantities computed here. The verb-type contrast describes the observed rows under standard errors that treat them as independent. The duration slope is further restricted to episodic responses and summarizes two choices made together. Neither coefficient has a causal interpretation under this design.

## Recap and check

1. Is $Y_i$ a probability? No. $Y_i$ is the observed binary random variable; $\pi_i$ is its conditional mean.
2. Does the inverse link repair an invalid response distribution? No. The family determines the response support and variance; the link only relates its mean to $\eta_i$.

The [exponential family](exponential-family.qmd) will let us see why several response distributions lead to related calculations without becoming the same probability model.
